faqs.question: What is a good short ghost story to tell on Halloween?
faqs.answer: 'The Tenant Below' in this post works for teenagers over 16 and adults: 110 words, under a minute at 130 words a minute, ending on three knocks you rap on the table. For children from 5, 'The Ghost Who Was Afraid of the Dark' is 88 words and ends on a sneeze, not a scare.

faqs.question: How long should a ghost story be for kids?
faqs.answer: For children aged 5 to 8, one to three minutes is enough; our two campfire stories are 88 and 108 words, under a minute each. Read two in a row rather than one long one, and finish on the gentler story.

faqs.question: What are some scary stories to tell on Halloween for teenagers?
faqs.answer: 'Seen' (108 words, ages 12+) is about a text to a dead grandmother's number that comes back as Seen, and 'The Practice Room' (116 words, ages 13+) is about a wrong note through a wall. For something longer, Dickens's 'The Signal-Man' runs about 39 minutes.

faqs.question: How do you tell a ghost story so it is actually scary?
faqs.answer: Read at about 130 words a minute, halve your pace for the two sentences before the jump, then pause for two full seconds before the last line. Use one light source and switch it off on the jump; a single clap or knock does more than any sound effect.

faqs.question: Why do people enjoy being scared by ghost stories?
faqs.answer: Shared fear is social. In a 2025 haunted-attraction study of 347 visitors, heart rates fell into step across the group, more synchrony went with more felt arousal, and close friends synchronised most.

faqs.question: Are M. R. James's ghost stories in the public domain?
faqs.answer: Yes in the UK, where James died in 1936 and the life-plus-70 term ran out at the end of 2006. In the US, his collections from 1904 to 1925 are public domain because works published in 1930 or earlier are free to use as of 2026; A Warning to the Curious (1925) entered on 1 January 2021.

faqs.question: Where can I read 'The Signal-Man' by Charles Dickens?
faqs.answer: It first appeared in the 1866 Christmas number of All the Year Round, Mugby Junction, which is Project Gutenberg ebook 27924. It is about 5,090 words, roughly 39 minutes read aloud.

faqs.question: Is a ghost story too scary for a five-year-old?
faqs.answer: It depends on the child, so read it yourself first and keep the lights partly on. Our two stories for ages 5 and 6 end on a sneeze and a trick-or-treat shout, with no death or injury, and you can skip the jump entirely.

faqs.question: Can I tell a ghost story over a video call?
faqs.answer: You can, but it lands less well. A 2026 study of 24 first-graders found that storytelling where the child joined in beat passive listening for word learning in person, and the gain disappeared when the same session ran over Zoom.

faqs.question: Can I send a recorded ghost story to someone for Halloween?
faqs.answer: Yes: the premium SubhSandesh Halloween page takes a voice note of up to 60 seconds, which at 130 words a minute holds any of the six stories here, and an unlock time can hold it until 31 October. It is a page for one person, not a party.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Ghost Stories: 6 Originals to Read Aloud by Age

Here are six original Halloween ghost stories written to be read aloud: two gentle campfire tales for children from 5, two for teenagers and two slow-burn stories for adults. Each takes under a minute at a calm 130 words a minute, with an age rating and a marked jump moment.

Expect to read from a phone in the dark: 48.3% of pages shared on SubhSandesh are opened on a phone, and each is viewed 11.1 times on average. After the stories: a timing table, how to tell one, and four public-domain classics with exact editions.

## What makes a ghost story work out loud?

A read-aloud ghost story is a short spoken tale in which one ordinary detail goes wrong, dread builds, and a single beat releases it. The release is usually a shared laugh.

That sharing is measurable. In a 2025 study led by Marc Andersen with Mathias Clasen, 347 visitors to a haunted attraction wore heart-rate monitors, and their [heart rates fell into step with each other](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40720311) over spans from 25 seconds to about 55 minutes, and close friends synchronised most.

## 6 original Halloween ghost stories to read aloud

Age ratings are our own judgement, so read each story yourself first.

### 1. The Ghost Who Was Afraid of the Dark (campfire, ages 5+)

Ages 5+, about 45 seconds, gentle. Jump: shout the sneeze, then laugh.

> Wisp was the smallest ghost in the lighthouse, and Wisp had a secret. Whenever the great lamp swung away, Wisp hid under a fishing net and shivered.
>
> One Halloween the lamp went out. Something came up the stairs: tap... tap... tap. The old ghosts dived under the net. Wisp floated to the top step, took the biggest breath a ghost can take, and...
>
> **"BOO-CHOO!"**
>
> It was only the keeper's cat. And the sneeze was so bright that the lamp blinked on again. Nobody called Wisp small after that.

### 2. The Pumpkin That Counted (campfire, ages 6+)

Ages 6+, about 50 seconds, gentle. Jump: clap on "Trick or treat!"

> On Mrs Okafor's porch sat a pumpkin that counted. This year eight children climbed the steps: a witch, a robot, two bats, a dinosaur, a mummy, a cat and one very small ghost. "Six. Seven. Eight," whispered the pumpkin.
>
> Then its candle flickered. "...Nine." The children turned round. There was no ninth child, only a long, thin shadow at the bottom of the steps with nobody standing on it. It crept up, one step at a time, and held out its hand...
>
> **"TRICK OR TREAT!"**
>
> It was the small ghost's shadow. It had run ahead because it wanted a sweet too. Mrs Okafor gave it a shadow-shaped one.

### 3. Seen (teen, ages 12+)

Ages 12+, about 50 seconds, eerie, not violent. Jump: tap the table on the buzz.

> Maya still texted her grandmother's old number on bad nights. "Got a B in chemistry." "Mum burned the dal again." The messages always said Delivered, nothing more.
>
> On Halloween she typed, "I miss you. It's cold here," and switched off the lamp. At 3:07 the room lit blue. One word had changed. Seen.
>
> Three grey dots appeared. They pulsed, stopped, pulsed again, slowly, the way her grandmother had always typed, one finger at a time.
>
> **The phone buzzed in her hand.**
>
> "Wear your coat."
>
> In the morning there was frost on every window in the street. Maya wore her coat. She never asked who had that number now.

### 4. The Practice Room (teen, ages 13+)

Ages 13+, about 55 seconds, mild dread. Jump: drop a book flat for the lid.

> Room 4 was the only practice room free after nine, so Dev took it every night in October. Through the wall, someone in Room 5 played the same piece and hit the same wrong note in bar 12.
>
> On the fourth night Dev played bar 12 properly, twice. Next door went quiet. The following night the piece came through the wall again, bar 12 perfect, and then the player copied Dev's warm-up, note for note.
>
> Dev went next door. Room 5 held a mop bucket and a framed photo of the class of 1961. A boy in the front row was holding sheet music.
>
> **Behind Dev, the piano lid slammed.**
>
> Pencilled inside it: "Bar 13 next."

### 5. The Glove (adults, 16+)

Ages 16+, about 45 seconds, no gore. Jump: whisper "warm", then grab a hand.

> On 1 October Hannah found a child's red glove pushed onto the railings at the end of her road, the way people leave lost things. On the second it was one railing closer to her house. On the third, closer again.
>
> By the thirtieth she could see it from her window, four houses down.
>
> On Halloween morning she opened the front door for the milk. The glove was on her door handle. She reached for it, meaning to bin it.
>
> **It was warm.**
>
> And from inside, small fingers closed around hers.

### 6. The Tenant Below (adults, 16+)

Ages 16+, about 50 seconds, building dread. Jump: knock three times.

> The flat was cheap because, the agent said, Mrs Hale downstairs banged on her ceiling with a broom after midnight. Priya went to bed at eleven. Even so, at 2:14 every night came three hard knocks under her floor.
>
> After a week she went down with biscuits to apologise. A neighbour frowned. "Mrs Hale moved to a care home in March. That flat's been empty since."
>
> Then Priya understood. Mrs Hale had heard footsteps up there for years. The knocks were never complaints. They were warnings.
>
> That night, at 2:13, the floorboards in her hallway began to creak, one step at a time, towards her bedroom door.
>
> **Knock. Knock. Knock.**

## Ghost stories by age: time, scare level and light

Word counts are our own. One original plus one classic fills a 45-minute evening.

| Tier | Stories | Words, and time at 130 wpm | Scare and jump | Light |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Campfire (5+) | 1, 2 | 88 and 108 words, under 1 minute each | Gentle: sneeze, clap | Lamp on low |
| Teen (12+) | 3, 4 | 108 and 116 words, under 1 minute each | Eerie: buzz, slam | One torch |
| Adult (16+) | 5, 6 | 91 and 110 words, under 1 minute each | Dread: whisper, knocks | One candle |
| Classics (10+) | 4 below | 3,730 to 5,670 words, 29 to 44 minutes | Dread, one comic | Torch for the reader |

## How to tell a scary story: pacing, pauses and light

Read at about 130 words a minute, halving the pace for the two sentences before the jump. Then stop for two full seconds: the pause frightens, the shout only releases it.

A 2024 University of Bristol study of 60 adults found [narrative about 10 times as predictive of heart rate](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11530447) as the sights and sounds on screen, even for listeners who only heard the audio.

- **Light:** one source, below your face or behind the listeners, switched off on the jump.
- **Voice:** whisper the line before the jump, then go full volume for one word.
- **Children:** let a young listener guess what is on the stairs and finish the line. In a 2026 Tel Aviv University study of 24 first-graders, mean age 6.9, [storytelling with the child joining in beat passive listening](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13246770) for word learning, but the gain vanished over Zoom.

## 4 public-domain classics to read aloud on Halloween

All four authors died before 1937, so these are out of copyright in the UK (life plus 70 years) and the US (published 1930 or earlier, as of 2026).

- **"The Signal-Man", Charles Dickens (1812–1870):** from the 1866 Christmas number of All the Year Round, in [Mugby Junction, Gutenberg ebook 27924](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/27924). About 5,090 words, 39 minutes; a signalman sees a figure before each disaster. Ages 12+.
- **"An Evening's Entertainment", M. R. James (1862–1936):** in [A Warning to the Curious (1925), Gutenberg ebook 66881](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/66881). About 4,810 words, 37 minutes; a grandmother tells fireside tales with "a pleasing terror". Ages 14+. James's UK copyright expired at the end of 2006, and the 1925 book entered the US public domain on 1 January 2021.
- **"The Ghost and the Bone-Setter", J. S. Le Fanu (1814–1873):** a comic Irish tale from the late 1830s, in [The Purcell Papers, Volume 1, Gutenberg ebook 509](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/509). About 3,730 words, 29 minutes. Ages 10+.
- **"The Spectre Bridegroom", Washington Irving (1783–1859):** in The Sketch-Book of Geoffrey Crayon, 1819–20, Gutenberg ebook 2048. About 5,670 words, 44 minutes; the "ghost" is a living suitor. Ages 10+.

## Sending a ghost story to one person who isn't in the room

Both SubhSandesh Halloween pages are for one person, not a party.

The [interactive Halloween card with a flashlight letter](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) suits a child or a friend: they read your letter by flashlight in a dark attic, so story 1 can be the letter. Its Kids tone has no jump scares; it takes about 5 minutes.

The [cinematic Halloween page with a 60-second voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) suits a partner or best friend far away. Sixty seconds at 130 words a minute holds any story above, a spirit radio plays it, and an optional unlock time can hold the page until Saturday 31 October 2026 or Sunday 31 October 2027. It takes about 10 minutes, but on our apology dashboard the median gap from first save to last edit is 2.5 hours, so start a day early.

For someone who would rather hear you introduce a song, a [radio-show dedication in your own voice](https://subhsandesh.in/dedication) fits better.

## When a ghost story is the wrong choice

Skip the teen and adult tiers for anyone under 12, and read every story first. Story 3 involves a grandmother who has died, so leave it out for a recently bereaved listener.

A link also scares less than a room. Our pages are English-only, and a 60-second voice note cannot hold a 37-minute classic.

## Sources

- [Scared together](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40720311), Emotion, 28 July 2025 (abstract read).
- [Narrative predicts cardiac synchrony in audiences](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11530447), Scientific Reports, 2 November 2024.
- [Word learning and neural synchrony during children's storytelling](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13246770), npj Science of Learning, 28 March 2026.
- [Mugby Junction](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/27924), 1866.
- [A Warning to the Curious](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/66881), 1925.
- [The Purcell Papers, Volume 1](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/509).

Field study at a haunted house attraction: N = 347 visitors aged 18-63 (254 in HR analyses); HR synchrony emerged across timescales from 25 s to ~55 min; greater synchrony associated with greater subjective arousal; socially close dyads synchronised more. ABSTRACT ONLY read via the Europe PMC REST API; the full text is not open.

Hammond, Armstrong, Thomas, Dalmaijer, Bull & Gilchrist, Scientific Reports (CC BY). N = 60 participants, largely University of Bristol students and staff, watched or only heard a 55-minute BBC drama episode; heart-rate synchrony was driven by the narrative alone, and narrative was approximately 10 times as predictive of heart rate as low-level audio-visual saliency. Full text read via Europe PMC.

Besser Ilan, Shavit, Zohar & Jaffe-Dax, npj Science of Learning (CC BY). Tel Aviv University; 24 first-graders analysed (age 6.9 +/- 0.3 years). Storytelling with scaffolding (child actively engaged) improved word learning over passive listening and was associated with higher teacher-child neural synchrony; the learning benefit disappeared when the sessions ran remotely over Zoom. Full text read via Europe PMC.

Dickens et al., Mugby Junction (Gutenberg text of the Chapman and Hall 1898 edition of the extra Christmas number of All the Year Round, 1866). Contains 'The Signal-Man' (No. 1 Branch Line): 5,094 words by plain count of the Gutenberg text, 39 minutes at 130 wpm (our estimate). Dickens 1812-1870 per Gutenberg author record. Text read.

M. R. James, A Warning to the Curious (London: Edward Arnold, 1925; preface dated September 1925). 'An Evening's Entertainment': about 4,810 words by plain count, 37 minutes at 130 wpm; opens on the fireside grandam who 'inspires her audience with a pleasing terror'. James 1862-1936 per Gutenberg author record: UK term (life + 70) expired end of 2006; a 1925 publication entered the US public domain on 1 January 2021 (95-year term). Text read.

J. Sheridan Le Fanu, The Purcell Papers, Volume 1 (with a memoir by A. P. Graves). 'The Ghost and the Bone-Setter': 3,730 words by plain count, 29 minutes at 130 wpm; the memoir lists it among Le Fanu's humorous Irish stories in the Dublin University Magazine of the late 1830s ('1837 or 1838'). The Gutenberg text prints no edition date, so none is claimed. Le Fanu 1814-1873. Text read.

structuralLimitations: No Halloween usage data exists in facts.md; the three first-party figures are platform-wide and the 2.5-hour edit gap is labelled in the body as sampled on the apology dashboard.
Scared together (Emotion 2025) was read as abstract only; the body cites only abstract figures (N = 347, 25 s to ~55 min, closeness).
Irving's 'The Spectre Bridegroom' is named with its Gutenberg ebook number (2048) but not linked, to keep outbound links at 6; its 5,670-word count is our plain count of the Gutenberg text (5,666).

Prompt framing check: the row notes suggested M. R. James's PD status needed verification; Gutenberg's author record gives 1862-1936, so UK (life + 70) expired end of 2006, and the 1925 collection used here is US public domain since 1 January 2021. The Le Fanu Gutenberg text prints no edition date, and its memoir names 'Sir Robert Ardagh' (1838) as his first published story, so the post says only 'late 1830s' for 'The Ghost and the Bone-Setter'.
Age ratings for the six stories and the four classics are editorial judgement, said so in the body; no rating scheme was cited.
